title: Roasted Corn with Ube
localName: Agbado yinyan — roast corn and African pear
author: Ozoz Adeniyi
desc: Fresh corn roasted on hot coals and African pear either roasted alongside or softened in freshly boiled water — starch and fat, the same logic as tortilla and avocado.
longDesc: This is the rainy season on a Nigerian roadside: a cob of corn roasted over coals until the kernels are toasty and fragrant, and ube — the African pear — either roasted beside it or dropped into freshly boiled water to soften. Ube cooked tastes, by one good description, like avocado cut through with green olives and a touch of cream, and the pairing is not arbitrary. It is starch plus a fatty fruit, which is the same structural logic as corn tortillas and guacamole. No quantities are published and none are needed.
equipment: A bowl, if softening the ube in water
steps: Strip the husks from the corn.
Roast the cobs over hot coals, turning, until the kernels are golden and toasty and smell fragrant — around 15 to 20 minutes.
For the ube, either roast it on the coals alongside the corn, or put it in a bowl and cover with freshly boiled water until it softens.
Serve the hot corn with the softened ube, pulling the flesh off the pear's stone.
Add a piece of fresh coconut if you have it, and salt to taste.
chefTips: Ube must be roasted on hot coals or soaked in freshly boiled water before eating. Raw it is unpleasant and almost inedible.
Freshly boiled water, not hot tap water. It needs real heat to soften.
Turn the corn constantly. Roast corn burns in patches if you leave it, and the burnt patches are bitter rather than smoky.
Fresh corn, in season. This is a rainy-season food in Nigeria and out of season both components are poor.
The pairing works because it is starch plus a fatty fruit — the same reason tortillas go with avocado. Knowing that is what stops it seeming like an odd combination.
Fresh coconut makes it a trio, which is how it is often sold.
No quantities exist for this in any source and none are needed — one cob and one ube per person is the street-side unit.
commonMistakes: Using lukewarm water to soften it.
Leaving the corn still on the coals until it chars.
Trying it out of season with old corn.
Treating the ube as a garnish rather than half the dish.
sources: Adapted from 'Nigerian Street Food: Golden Roasted Corn with Ube', published on kitchenbutterfly.com, 10 July 2018. ATTRIBUTION: the byline prints as the site name; the site is credited, with Ozoz Sokoh noted as proprietor. Local name as printed: Agbado yinyan.

NO INGREDIENT LIST, NO METHOD AND NO QUANTITIES appear on the page — it is an essay rather than a recipe, and that is stated here rather than disguised. What it gives is the preparation requirement, the flavour description and the rationale for the pairing, all of which are reproduced below. The roasting time in the steps above is a practical estimate and is labelled as such, not sourced.

UBE PREPARATION, verbatim and the one piece of load-bearing instruction: ube 'must be roasted on hot coals or soaked in freshly boiled water to eat.' Cooked, it tastes 'like avocado, cut through with green olives and a touch of cream.'
ON THE CORN, verbatim: 'fresh golden, toasted kernels fall of hot cobs, toasty and fragrant with heat.' The corn variety is not specified.

THE PAIRING RATIONALE, verbatim and the reason this entry is worth having: 'There are many ways one could eat roasted corn. With ube seems the most natural choice.' She draws a parallel to 'the building blocks for corn tacos and guacamole' — starch plus a fatty fruit, the same structural logic as tortilla and avocado. That is her mechanism for why the pairing is not arbitrary.
SEASON as printed: rainy season; 'summer and winter to other parts of the world.' A TRIO including fresh coconut is also named on the page.

WHY THIS IS PUBLISHED DESPITE HAVING NO QUANTITIES: it is two whole ingredients cooked over coals, so there is nothing to get wrong by weight, and the one instruction that matters — that ube must be heated before eating — is clearly stated. The gap is a documentation gap rather than a safety or accuracy one.

A RELATED GAP: boli or bole, roasted plantain with fish and groundnut, was specifically sought and NO acceptable named source was found. The best-ranked results were on the avoid list or unverifiable. Kitchen Butterfly's 'Nigerian Street Food: Bole & Fish' was located but not retrieved. Boli is therefore not published in this collection.
storage: Eat at once. Roast corn goes tough within the hour.
reheating: Back on the coals briefly. Never the microwave.
healthBenefits: Ube is high in monounsaturated fat, similar in profile to avocado.
Fresh corn supplies fibre, folate and lutein.
Nothing is added — no oil, no sugar.
culturalNote: Roast corn and ube is the most seasonal food in Nigeria — it appears with the rains, is sold from charcoal braziers at the roadside for a few months, and then goes. Ube is Dacryodes edulis, the African pear, and it has no real substitute: the combination of a starchy cob and a soft, faintly resinous, oily fruit is particular to this part of the world.
